title: Anniversaries

jokes.text: "And the groom wore a butt so perfect it could make an angel hang itself."
jokes.setup: A straight, formal newspaper-style wedding announcement is being read aloud, establishing an elevated, official tone.
jokes.punchline: The final line veers into absurdly hyperbolic, darkly comedic praise of Ben's butt — completely tonally incongruous with the rest of the announcement.
jokes.explanation: This is a cold-open gem. The formal structure of the wedding announcement is meticulously maintained until the final phrase, which delivers a tonal whiplash of the highest order. 'Could make an angel hang itself' is genuinely original — an extreme hyperbole that veers dark while remaining absurd. It's quintessentially Leslie: obsessive adoration of Ben expressed with unhinged intensity. The economy is excellent; the whole joke is in that final clause. The follow-up 'You wrote this, didn't you?' / 'They cut it way down' / 'Thank God' is the perfect landing. Justifies the 8+ because very few jokes in an episode open with this level of originality and character-specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: On this day, two souls unite in holy matrimony. Leslie Knope and Ben Wyatt, bound by love's eternal flame, embark upon a journey of passion and devotion.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: Ben Wyatt is so attractive that the sun became jealous and threw itself into a black hole. The moon wept for seven years. Stars began falling from the sky, unable to bear the shame of being outshined.

jokes.text: "You wrote this, didn't you?" / "I did." / "They cut it way down." / "Thank God."
jokes.setup: The absurd butt-praising announcement has just been read aloud.
jokes.punchline: Ben confirms Leslie wrote it, reveals it was even longer, and his response is pure relief — implying the original was even more unhinged.
jokes.explanation: A perfect tag to the cold-open joke. 'Thank God' as Ben's only reaction implies the uncut version was even more mortifying, which amplifies the original joke retroactively. The economy is impeccable — two words do enormous work. Ben's deadpan resignation is deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Two souls, intertwined like vines upon a trellis of destiny, joined in matrimonial bliss beneath the stars that whispered their names since the dawn of time...

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's what I wrote.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Thank God they edited it.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: she always tells Ben no gifts, Ben always believes her, and she surprises him every year with 'the best gift of all time' — and he makes 'the cutest, dopiest face... Wha-a-a-at?'
jokes.setup: Leslie describes their anniversary rules: no gifts.
jokes.punchline: She immediately reveals she has never followed this rule, and Ben always falls for it. Her impression of Ben's dopey surprised face ('Wha-a-a-at?') is the comedic peak.
jokes.explanation: Classic talking-head structure: statement of rule, immediate undermining of rule. The physical impression of Ben's dopy face ('Wha-a-a-at?') is a strong character moment and sets up the episode-long runner about who surprises whom. The character integration is high — this is very specifically Leslie's brand of loving scheming.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: His face was like... *makes exaggerated dopey expression with mouth hanging open and eyes wide*

jokes.text: Ben's talking head: he got Leslie the most amazing gift ever, giving it to her one day early so SHE will make 'that stupid face.'
jokes.setup: Immediately after Leslie's talking head where she gloats about always surprising Ben with gifts.
jokes.punchline: Ben has independently hatched the same counter-strategy and is equally convinced he'll win. The structural juxtaposition of the two confessionals creates the joke.
jokes.explanation: The edit between these two confessionals is the joke. Both characters have secretly planned gifts; both think they'll be the one to surprise the other. It's a perfect comedic structure — setup in one talking head, immediate ironic counterpoint in the next. The runner pays off beautifully throughout the episode. High marks for structure and how the mockumentary format is weaponized.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm going to surprise Leslie. She has no idea what's coming.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm going to make her look so stupid.

jokes.text: Ben's confessional mirror: 'I'm not gonna make my stupid surprise face this year... So she's gonna make the face this year. She will make that stupid face!'
jokes.setup: We just saw Leslie describe the 'dopey face' Ben makes. Now Ben's confessional reveals he's planning to flip the script.
jokes.punchline: Ben's escalating determination — 'She WILL make that stupid face!' — mirrors Leslie's exact same scheming energy, revealing they are perfectly matched in their competitive gift-giving neuroses.
jokes.explanation: The immediate structural callback to Leslie's confessional — same joke, mirrored perspective — reveals the comic truth that they are identical in their neurotic competitiveness. Ben calling it 'that stupid face' (the face Leslie lovingly described) adds an extra layer. The escalating 'She WILL make that stupid face!' mimics Leslie's own over-the-top intensity, making the callback feel earned rather than repetitive.

dialogue.speaker: Radio Announcer
dialogue.line: This program is brought to you by the Foundation Foundation, a foundation dedicated to promoting foundations. The Foundation Foundation: because foundations need foundations too.

jokes.text: "...and the Richard and Lois Wallenberg Foundation Foundation... dedicated to the idea that all human beings deserve a chance to hear about foundations."
jokes.setup: A public radio sponsorship announcement reads off foundation names in the expected dry, formal manner.
jokes.punchline: 'Foundation Foundation' is an absurd double-word name, and the mission statement — dedicated to humans hearing about foundations — is circular self-referential nonsense delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: A sharp absurdist joke embedded in a very specific parody of NPR-style underwriting. The recursive logic of 'Foundation Foundation dedicated to people hearing about foundations' is genuinely clever. Slightly docked on character integration because it's a radio station gag rather than tied to any main character's voice.

jokes.text: Derry Murbles and August Clementine argue about whether it's the 'Pawnee-Eagleton' or 'Eagleton-Pawnee' merger, followed by Derry 'apologizing for his co-host's sudden and violent outburst just now.'
jokes.setup: The radio show introduces its co-hosts as a result of the merger.
jokes.punchline: A completely minor naming dispute is characterized as a 'violent outburst' — the deadpan absurdity of treating a trivial disagreement as a major incident.
jokes.explanation: A tight joke that models the entire merger conflict in miniature. The deadpan escalation — calling a quiet disagreement about word order a 'violent outburst' — perfectly captures the absurd pettiness of inter-town rivalry. The joke does real thematic work for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: August
dialogue.line: It's actually called the 'merger,' not the 'violent outburst.'

dialogue.speaker: Derry
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I just had a violent outburst!

jokes.text: August Clementine's "Absorb the aggression, Derry. Absorb the aggression." after Leslie finishes the show's catchphrase herself.
jokes.setup: Leslie completes the show's 'Thought for your thoughts' catchphrase before Derry can, stepping on his hosting moment.
jokes.punchline: August's calm, condescending instruction to Derry to 'absorb the aggression' treats the tiny slight as a meditative exercise in patience.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'Absorb the aggression' is a funny piece of deadpan wisdom that lands because it's so overly therapeutic for such a tiny incident. Quotable enough to stick.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Treat yo' self!

dialogue.speaker: August
dialogue.line: Actually, I think you mean 'treat yourself' with proper pronunciation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, it's 'treat yo' self' — that's the whole thing!

dialogue.speaker: August
dialogue.line: Well, if you say so. I'm sure your way is just fine. Really great. Wonderful.

jokes.text: "It was a pizza whose crust was stuffed with little pizzas. And the crust of those little pizzas was made of chocolate."
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions the discontinued pizza-stuffed-crust pizza.
jokes.punchline: She explains the Inception-like recursive pizza structure, then adds that the inner crust was chocolate — an escalation that goes one step too far into glorious absurdity.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best pure joke structure. The first sentence is funny; the second sentence makes it exceptional. 'A pizza whose crust was stuffed with little pizzas' is already a recursive absurdity, but adding 'and the crust of those little pizzas was made of chocolate' takes the logical escalation to an insane third level. It's the Pawnee food mythology at its finest — specific, escalating, and internally consistent in its own lunatic way. Earns the 8+ because the two-beat structure is textbook escalation comedy executed with precision.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know, I think this merged show is really... quiet and arcane.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Did you just call our show boring and weird?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No! I meant... it's got a certain... understated charm?

jokes.text: "Yes, there were some bumps and bruises. And a brief rash of arson. And a rather large-scale brawl at the dump."
jokes.setup: Leslie is defending the merger as having gone well.
jokes.punchline: She casually lists escalating incidents of civic chaos — arson and a brawl — as minor footnotes to an otherwise positive narrative.
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie structure: optimistic spin on increasingly alarming information. The deadpan delivery of 'a brief rash of arson' as a euphemism is the key laugh, and the escalation to a dump brawl lands the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The anger level in this town right now is comparable to when Pizza Hut discontinued their pizza-stuffed-crust pizza.

jokes.text: August says "Scoff." out loud instead of actually scoffing. Derry: "Did you just say the word 'scoff'?"
jokes.setup: Leslie has declared the merger is going well. August wants to express disdain.
jokes.punchline: Instead of scoffing, he literally verbalizes the action word 'scoff' — a bizarre, overly literal choice that a radio host might make, perhaps because it's audio-only, but which is profoundly strange in person.
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely original joke. The concept of a radio host narrating his own emotional reactions instead of performing them is a sharp, specific absurdist premise that's both character-rooted and conceptually fresh. The follow-up 'Did you just say the word scoff?' earns the laugh even further by having another character acknowledge how bizarre it is. Justifies 8+ because it's a concept you don't see often, executed with perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But what if we took it further? What if we stuffed the crust with another pizza?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And that pizza has a chocolate crust stuffed with dessert pizza. It's pizza all the way down, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's the most ridiculous thing I've ever heard.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You say that, but I've already ordered the ingredients.

jokes.text: August: "I now have to share my studio with a fatuous twerp who shall remain nameless." Derry: "This twerp has a name. And it's August N'gutu Liebowitz-Clementine."
jokes.setup: August insults Derry indirectly by saying 'who shall remain nameless.'
jokes.punchline: Derry responds by... naming August. The indignant self-identification as the insulted party, complete with his full absurd name, is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed little reversal. Derry's full name 'August N'gutu Liebowitz-Clementine' is funny in its own right — an absurdly multicultural mash-up — and the delivery of it as a defiant comeback adds character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: The merger is going to be great for both towns.

dialogue.speaker: August
dialogue.line: Scoff.

jokes.text: Ben's talking-head theorizing that Larry's gorgeous wife Gayle might still be under hypnosis — and that saying 'nutmeg' might snap her out of it.
jokes.setup: Ben explains he asked Larry for anniversary advice because Larry has the most successful marriage he knows — to a surprisingly beautiful woman.
jokes.punchline: Ben spins an elaborate hypnosis-accident theory and wonders if saying 'nutmeg' would cause Gayle to 'wake up and start screaming.' The specificity of 'nutmeg' as the magic word is the absurdist peak.
jokes.explanation: A long-running Parks gag (Larry's inexplicably attractive wife) is given a fresh, creative spin. Rather than just commenting on the mismatch, Ben constructs a detailed conspiracy theory with 'nutmeg' as the magic deprogramming word. The specificity of 'nutmeg' makes it: any other word would be less funny. High character integration — this is Ben's brand of earnest, nerdy overthinking. Approaches 8+ because it's building on an established running gag with a genuinely fresh premise.

dialogue.speaker: August
dialogue.line: Scoff.

dialogue.speaker: Derry
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, what?

jokes.text: Shelter worker: "What kind of pet are you interested in adopting? We have dogs, cats, rabbits." / Worker 2 (presumably Tom): "Um, I work here, so, legally, you can adopt me."
jokes.setup: Standard shelter intake question listing adoptable animals.
jokes.punchline: An employee interrupts to offer himself as an adoptable option, citing a legal framework that doesn't exist.
jokes.explanation: A decent gag — the absurdist pivot of offering yourself as an adoptee is funny — but it's not deeply character-specific and the legal framing ('legally, you can adopt me') is the kind of joke that could be in many shows.

dialogue.speaker: August
dialogue.line: It's actually August Beauregard Van Der Meer-Schildkraut the Third.

jokes.text: Ron looking at the child's drawing of a dog: "So, like a banana made of spiders?"
jokes.setup: Ron and April are at an animal shelter. The children want a dog that looks like a specific drawing they made.
jokes.punchline: Ron's deadpan interpretation of the child's artwork — 'a banana made of spiders' — is both a commentary on children's drawing skills and an unexpectedly vivid image.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best single-line jokes. 'A banana made of spiders' is an extraordinarily specific and original image that works because it sounds exactly like what a child's scribbled dog could look like. The economy is perfect — five words that conjure a vivid, absurd picture. Ron's flat delivery makes it better. This is deeply character-specific: only Ron would process a child's art with this kind of clinical, unsentimental precision. Justifies 8+ easily.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: How did Larry even end up with someone like Tammy? She's so out of his league.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm serious. I've been thinking about this, and the only explanation is elaborate hypnosis. Like, he must have hypnotized her at some point. That's the only way it makes sense.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: He probably spent years perfecting his hypnotic technique, just waiting for the right moment to use it on an attractive woman. And somehow it worked.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's the only logical explanation for why someone like Tammy would marry Larry Gergich.

jokes.text: "I've said it before and I'll say it again, children are terrible artists. And artists are crooks."
jokes.setup: Following the banana-made-of-spiders line, continuing the theme of children's artistic incompetence.
jokes.punchline: Ron pivots from criticizing children's art to a sweeping condemnation of all artists as 'crooks' — a classic Ron Swanson worldview expansion.
jokes.explanation: The two-part construction is key: the first clause ('children are terrible artists') is straightforwardly Ron. The second clause ('and artists are crooks') broadens it into his entire anti-art philosophy — a non-sequitur that follows its own perfect internal logic. 'I've said it before and I'll say it again' signals this is a deeply held Ron Swanson belief, adding to its absurdity. Near-flawless character integration. Earns 8+ because it's both instantly quotable and perfectly character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm basically a pet. I have the same life span as a tortoise, I'm mostly quiet, and I only show affection to one person. You should adopt me. It's legal because I checked with the courts and they said 'please stop calling.'

jokes.text: Ron meets the shelter dog, immediately says 'Hello, dog. I'll take him.' That was easy.
jokes.setup: After the elaborate description of needing a specific dog and the child's drawing, they go to find the dog.
jokes.punchline: Ron's instant, unambiguous decision — no deliberation, no second-guessing — is the joke. 'That was easy' captures it perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Ron's directness as a character trait is used efficiently here. The setup made it seem like finding the right dog would be complex; Ron cuts through it in seconds. Good character integration, though not as inspired as the preceding Ron jokes.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This is a dog that eats other dogs and poops out skeletons.

jokes.text: Tom finds a note from Donna: "Why lie? I'm shopping. Back in an hour."
jokes.setup: Tom calls for Donna to help with adoption paperwork, apparently expecting her to be at her desk.
jokes.punchline: Donna left a note that is entirely honest about her truancy — she's not even pretending to have a work excuse. "Why lie?" is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: 'Why lie?' is a perfect character expression — Donna's complete lack of pretense or guilt about doing exactly what she wants. The note is two sentences and tells you everything about Donna Meagle. High character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That child has no future.

jokes.text: Radio caller: merger has caused a 'really bad trash problem.' Leslie: 'some confusion with garbage routes.' Caller: 'No, I mean Eagletonians are human garbage. And we should throw them in a dumpster. Kapow!'
jokes.setup: The caller appears to be making a legitimate complaint about sanitation services post-merger.
jokes.punchline: The 'trash problem' is revealed to be metaphorical — he means Eagletonians are garbage. The 'Kapow!' is an absurd finishing flourish.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed misdirection. Leslie's earnest policy response makes the pivot funnier. 'Kapow!' is wonderfully bizarre — the caller's self-punctuation for his own zinger.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Children are terrible artists. Their paintings look like they were made by drunk chimpanzees having a seizure. And honestly, if you think about it, all artists are just criminals who haven't been caught yet.

jokes.text: Second caller: 'I really like the merger, but I hate that Eagleton was forced to join Pawnee.' / Leslie: 'Well, that's what the merger is.' / Caller: 'Oh. Yeah, then I hate the merger.'
jokes.setup: A caller seems to be expressing qualified support for the merger.
jokes.punchline: The caller's stated position collapses immediately when Leslie points out their preferred scenario IS the merger — they just didn't know it. Their instant reversal to 'Oh. Yeah, then I hate the merger' is a perfect beat.
jokes.explanation: A tight three-line joke with excellent structure. The comedy comes from the caller's complete intellectual dishonesty — they don't actually care about the substance, only the tribal allegiance. Good observational comedy about small-town politics.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Donna, where have you been? I've been looking all over for you.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm out of the office. Check my out-of-office message.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What does it say?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: It says I'm out of the office and I don't care about your email. I will delete it. I don't know who you are. Stop emailing me.

jokes.text: Third radio caller turns out to be Andy. Leslie: 'I don't know who this is, but I agree.' / Andy: 'It's Andy!' / 'I'm on the radio!'
jokes.setup: An anonymous caller expresses enthusiastic support for the merger and Leslie.
jokes.punchline: It's Andy — and his excitement at being on the radio is a more immediate thrill than the topic at hand.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm on the radio!' lands because of Andy's childlike enthusiasm — the medium is more exciting to him than the message. Character-specific and warm.

dialogue.speaker: Radio caller
dialogue.line: Yeah, we got a real trash problem here since the merger. Garbage everywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Radio caller
dialogue.line: I mean, people are garbage. Kapow!

jokes.text: August Clementine: 'And I talked last. Good day.' — ending the radio show by claiming victory for speaking last.
jokes.setup: Derry signs off with his name, August follows with his name.
jokes.punchline: August adds 'And I talked last. Good day.' — treating the order of sign-offs as a competitive win.
jokes.explanation: A tight little button on the radio show segment. August's pettiness about talking last is perfectly in character and a good miniaturized version of the Pawnee-Eagleton rivalry dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Radio caller
dialogue.line: I love the merger idea, but I don't think Eagleton should be forced to join Pawnee. They should have a choice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: But that IS the merger. Eagleton is joining Pawnee.

dialogue.speaker: Radio caller
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, then I'm against it.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Is this land mine still functional?' / April: 'Partially.' / Tom: 'Because I want to blow up Donna's desk so I can teach her a lesson about what happens when you skip work.'
jokes.setup: Tom is frustrated that Donna left work without notice.
jokes.punchline: His solution to a workplace HR issue is to detonate a landmine — and April's 'Partially' suggests they actually have one nearby.
jokes.explanation: April's deadpan 'Partially' is the key laugh — she's not alarmed or surprised by the landmine's presence, just offering factual status. Good character comedy for both: Tom's impulsive overreaction and April's casual acceptance of dangerous objects.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, and another thing—Leslie is amazing and—wait, did I just say that out loud? Oh no, oh no, oh no. I'm so bad at this.

jokes.text: Tom's talking head: Instead of confronting Donna directly, he 'very maturely' left an anonymous Yelp review as 'Stopped by to adopt a dog, but the employee, Donna Meagle, was nowhere to be found. Thanks for nothing, Donna Meagle. Booooo!' — with five O's.
jokes.setup: Ron told Tom to be 'mature, direct, and firm' with Donna.
jokes.punchline: Tom interprets this as an anonymous Yelp review calling her out by full name — the opposite of mature, direct (it's anonymous), and only technically 'firm.' The detail of 'five O's' in 'Booooo' is the comedic peak.
jokes.explanation: The ironic gap between Ron's advice and Tom's interpretation is the engine of this joke. 'Booooo! With five O's' is a perfect detail — it shows Tom took real effort to craft this passive-aggressive anonymous review while simultaneously outing himself with the name 'Donna Meagle' twice. It's both a perfect Tom Haverford character moment and a sharp satire of petty online behavior. High character integration earns the 8+.

dialogue.speaker: August
dialogue.line: Well, I guess that means I get the last word.

jokes.text: Donna reads the Yelp review and says 'Oh, my God, that sucks. Just have to work harder, I guess, huh?' — completely unbothered — before pivoting to hunting down the reviewer.
jokes.setup: Tom's anonymous Yelp review has been discovered by Donna.
jokes.punchline: Donna's initial reaction is cheerful acceptance of the critique, then immediately pivots to threatening to 'hunt you down' — the whiplash between compliance and aggression is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Donna's response is perfectly in character — brief, performative self-reflection followed by immediate vindictiveness. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Can we get a land mine for the office? I want to put it under Jerry's desk.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, no.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Not to actually blow him up. Just as a threat. He'd be so careful where he stepped.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Don't be upset. No one listens to the radio. I wasn't even listening. I was listening to podcasts. Podcasts are great. Radio is boring.'
jokes.setup: Tom is upset about the bad Yelp review. Leslie tries to comfort him by dismissing radio's relevance.
jokes.punchline: Leslie — who just appeared ON radio — casually declares radio boring and podcasts superior. The meta-irony of a character on a radio show dismissing radio is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Good self-undermining irony — Leslie's blissful lack of awareness that she just participated in the very medium she's dismissing. Character-consistent and tight.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Kyle took me to Scherzinger's Funeral Home for our date.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Five stars. Great ambiance, very romantic. The embalming fluid really complemented the decay.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I cried the whole time, but not because of Kyle.

jokes.text: Larry keeps trying to show Leslie something, is dismissed, tries again, is dismissed again with 'Larry! What are you still doing here?' — Larry retreats with 'Aw, jeez. Okay.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to show Leslie Ben's surprise gift but can't break through her stress.
jokes.punchline: Larry's repeated deflections and final defeated 'Aw, jeez. Okay.' — he's carrying this huge secret and is completely powerless to deliver it.
jokes.explanation: The perennial Parks gag of Larry being dismissed and overlooked. It's deeply character-specific but not particularly original at this point in the series. The dramatic irony — he's the only one with the key to the episode's main plotline — gives it some extra dimension.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm writing a fake one-star review. 'This restaurant is a nightmare. The waiter brought me water I didn't ask for. Boooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooo.'

jokes.text: Andy: 'You look really old in this picture.' / Ben: 'Andy, this is a picture of us.' / Andy: 'This is a picture of an elderly couple. Rosie and Doug DeMarco.'
jokes.setup: Andy and Ben are looking at a newspaper photo together.
jokes.punchline: Andy has apparently been studying the wrong picture for long enough to conclude he looks 'really old' — revealing his complete lack of basic observational skill.
jokes.explanation: A quick, tight gag that works because of Andy's particular brand of cheerful obliviousness. The reveal is well-structured and the character integration is high — this is exactly how Andy processes information.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Booooo.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's seven O's, by the way. I counted.

jokes.text: "I'm afraid they're gonna rely too heavily on CGI. And I'm carrying it all in my shoulders."
jokes.setup: Ben needs to explain why he wants a couples massage even though Leslie can't make it. He mentions being 'kind of tense lately.'
jokes.punchline: The source of his tension is anxiety about the upcoming Star Wars sequel's production choices — and he has physically manifested this in his shoulders.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly calibrated Ben Wyatt joke. His nerd anxiety about Star Wars CGI being 'carried in his shoulders' is specific enough to be hilarious — it's the exact level of detail a deeply nerdy person would fixate on. The physical manifestation of a film production concern as bodily tension is a great absurdist step. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm gonna find whoever wrote this and break their legs.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I don't care if it's anonymous. I will find them.

jokes.text: Ben, somewhat defeated, asks Larry: "Larry, would you like to get a couples massage with me?" Larry: "I would love to."
jokes.setup: The masseur points out Ben paid for a couple but is alone.
jokes.punchline: Ben's obvious reluctance as he invites Larry, and Larry's wholehearted, delighted acceptance — Larry's gratitude for any inclusion makes it tender and funny simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in performance — Ben's defeated pause before offering and Larry's instant, enthusiastic 'I would love to.' Larry's sincerity makes it both funny and a little poignant.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wow, you look really old in this photo.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not even me.

jokes.text: April: 'Are we sure we should do this? Last time we scared an old person, Larry had a heart attack. That was awesome. He farted so much.'
jokes.setup: The group is about to visit the elderly DeMarcos.
jokes.punchline: April's anecdote about Larry's heart attack is framed with 'That was awesome. He farted so much.' — treating a medical emergency as entertainment and fixating on the flatulence.
jokes.explanation: Quintessential April Ludgate: genuine concern about a practical danger (they might scare an old person) combined with warm nostalgia for the most disturbing aspect of the incident. 'He farted so much' as her fondest memory of someone's cardiac event is perfectly in character. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm having an epiphany! Look at me, I'm sweating through my blouse!

jokes.text: Mrs. DeMarco: 'All right. How much money did we win?' / Leslie: 'Oh, no, you didn't win any money, you won something better than money.' / Mrs. DeMarco: 'So no money.'
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives to celebrate the DeMarcos' anniversary with an oversized novelty check.
jokes.punchline: Rosie immediately deflates Leslie's 'something better than money' with a flat restatement: 'So no money.' The elderly woman's unimpressed pragmatism is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured three-line joke. The giant novelty check creates a false expectation of money, Leslie offers a redemptive frame, Rosie strips it away in four words. The economy is outstanding — 'So no money' is the perfect punchline length.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I have so much tension in my shoulders from stress.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Stress about what?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I've been really worried about whether Batman could actually fly the Batplane.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not real.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know it's not real, but my shoulders don't.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I'm now just realizing how misleading this giant check is.' / Tom: 'Told you.'
jokes.setup: Rosie has just exposed that the giant check implies a cash prize.
jokes.punchline: Tom apparently warned Leslie about this and is now vindicated. Leslie's delayed self-awareness paired with Tom's smug 'Told you' is the beat.
jokes.explanation: A good tag to the previous joke. Tom's satisfaction is character-appropriate. The 'I'm now just realizing' construction is a nice Leslie self-awareness beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Hey Larry, um, I have a couples massage scheduled for tomorrow and my partner can't make it. Would you maybe want to... I mean, if you're not busy, we could just get massages together?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: ...What?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's not weird. People do it all the time. It's just relaxing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Ben, I don't think that's a good idea.

jokes.text: 'Thank you. Now is not the time. We... Hey! Hey! We'll give you some money. Okay? Here, here's some money. Everybody give 'em money.' / 'I got football cards, and a travel mouthwash.'
jokes.setup: The DeMarcos are unimpressed with a non-monetary prize and Leslie's event.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's composure breaks; she starts physically collecting money from the group. Andy's contribution is football cards and travel mouthwash — the specific uselessness of his offering is the comedic peak.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's unraveling into ad-hoc charity collection is a good comedic beat, but it's Andy's non-sequitur pocket inventory of 'football cards and a travel mouthwash' that elevates the moment. Very character-specific for Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, Larry had a medical emergency? That's awesome!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's not awesome, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, I know, I'm sorry. I just mean, like, he's gonna have the best story to tell. 'Oh, I had a heart attack and then I farted.' That's gold!

jokes.text: Donna to her hacker: 'I'm about to come down on this dude like Thor's hammer Mjolnir. I'm about to go Mjolnir on his ass!'
jokes.setup: Donna has tracked down who left her a bad Yelp review.
jokes.punchline: Donna's threat escalates from the metaphor 'like Thor's hammer Mjolnir' to the verb 'go Mjolnir on his ass' — treating the Norse god's weapon as a common verb.
jokes.explanation: Donna's pop-culture threat vocabulary is a good character joke. The escalation from metaphor to verb ('go Mjolnir on his ass') is a nice comic choice — she's so committed to the reference she's created a new word. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So you're going to be getting a check for $5,000, which is really life-changing money. You could pay off debts, or take a trip, or finally get that thing fixed that's been broken in your house for years.

dialogue.speaker: Rosie
dialogue.line: We're going to spend it all on lottery tickets.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh. Okay. Well, that's... that's one option.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: inspired by the Yelp thing, he's been composing strongly-worded letters to a vegetable farm, European ambassadors, a cologne manufacturer, and a nonfat frozen yogurt bar.
jokes.setup: Ron has discovered a use for the internet — writing complaint letters.
jokes.punchline: The list of targets escalates from the mundane (vegetable farm) to the geopolitically bizarre (European ambassadors) and back to the petty (frozen yogurt bar). Each target is a window into Ron's specific grievances.
jokes.explanation: The list of targets is perfectly Ron: his complaints span from deeply personal culinary grievances to the geopolitical. 'European ambassadors' in this context is a wonderful non-sequitur. Sets up the frozen yogurt joke beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna give you guys my Blockbuster membership card. It's still active, I think. You can rent movies for free, probably forever.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And I'm gonna throw in my collection of outdated celebrity gossip magazines. You'll learn some stuff about what Brangelina was up to in 2007.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, and this half-eaten sandwich from my car. It's a little fuzzy, but I think that's just seasoning.

jokes.text: "Dear frozen yogurt, you are the celery of desserts. Be ice cream or be nothing. Zero stars."
jokes.setup: Ron is writing Yelp-inspired strongly-worded letters. The frozen yogurt bar is one recipient.
jokes.punchline: 'You are the celery of desserts' is a perfectly constructed insult — it communicates total contempt using only food metaphors. 'Be ice cream or be nothing' is a Ron Swanson philosophical manifesto. 'Zero stars' is the perfect sign-off.
jokes.explanation: The single best joke in the episode and one of the best Ron Swanson lines in the series. 'You are the celery of desserts' is a masterpiece of comedic economy — it communicates Ron's entire food philosophy in seven words. Celery is perfect: it's not just bad, it's the food that exists as a placeholder for real food while pretending to be food. 'Be ice cream or be nothing' elevates it to a philosophical declaration that sounds like Ron Swanson's life motto applied to dessert. Every word is load-bearing. 'Zero stars' lands the format callback. This absolutely justifies a 9+ — it's an instantly quotable, perfectly constructed, deeply character-specific line that works as both food criticism and worldview statement.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: You know what? I don't care what that review said. I am like Thor. T-H-O-R. Thor. Not like some weak little Thor. I'm a full-powered, hammer-wielding, Asgardian Thor. Thor.

jokes.text: Ben's talking head: 'I watched Enchanted three times to get all the details right. And then another two times, because that movie is amazing.' / Larry: 'Oh, it really is.'
jokes.setup: Ben explains his research process for planning the anniversary surprise.
jokes.punchline: The first watch is research; the next two are pure enjoyment — and Larry's immediate, sincere agreement ('Oh, it really is.') doubles the confession.
jokes.explanation: A lovely two-beat joke. The first reveal (watching Enchanted for research) is funny; the second (watching it two more times out of genuine love) is the punchline. Larry's earnest 'Oh, it really is' turns it into a shared moment of sincere nerd confession. The character integration is high — Ben's blend of planning obsession and genuine enthusiasm for pop culture feels exactly right.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Dear Soda Fountain Enthusiast, I am writing to express my disgust with your frozen yogurt establishment. You call this yogurt? It is a frozen abomination, a dessert masquerading as culture. Your toppings bar is a monument to excess and poor decision-making, much like most of human civilization. The sprinkles are too colorful, the whipped cream too optimistic. This frozen disappointment has set back the cause of actual dairy by decades. I have seen more integrity in a bowl of sherbet. Sincerely, Ron Swanson.

jokes.text: Ben calls Leslie for a casual lunch, she turns him down. After hanging up, Ben realizes the waffle buffet and Hilary impersonator deposits are non-refundable.
jokes.setup: Ben's elaborate anniversary plan has collapsed because Leslie is busy with work.
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'waffle buffet' and 'Hilary impersonator' as planned elements reveals the extraordinary specificity of Ben's Leslie-tailored surprise — and the non-refundable deposits add comedic pathos.
jokes.explanation: A Hilary Clinton impersonator is exactly the kind of niche, hyper-personalized gift that only someone who truly knows Leslie Knope would arrange. The waffle buffet is equally perfect. The non-refundable deposits give it pathos. Good character integration for both Ben and Leslie (through Ben's knowledge of her).

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I've watched Enchanted five times.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Look, the first time was for Leslie. The second time was because Leslie wanted to watch it again. The third time I was just... in the room. But the last two times? That was all me. It's a good movie.

jokes.text: Tom: 'They're like the old version of iTunes. We're like the new version of iTunes, baby. We're gonna be here forever.' / Tom realizes: 'Oh, my God. I'm gonna die someday.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Andy are dismissing the relevance of the DeMarcos as old people.
jokes.punchline: Tom's metaphor — iTunes old vs. new — ironically captures exactly how ephemeral 'the new version' is, prompting his immediate existential crisis.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever joke. Tom's confidence in using 'new iTunes' as a symbol of eternal relevance is subverted by the fact that iTunes iterations are famously ephemeral and frustrating. The joke works on two levels: Tom's poor choice of metaphor, and his immediate confrontation with the implications of what it means to be 'the old version.' 'Oh, my God. I'm gonna die someday' is a perfect reaction — pure Tom Haverford, going from breezy dismissal to existential panic in a sentence. Earns 8+ for originality and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm trying to recreate that scene from The Princess Bride where Westley says 'As you wish.' So I thought I'd say something romantic in Old English or whatever.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Hark, fair maiden, thy beauty doth... um... shine brightly?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I read online that period language is romantic. I'm not good at this.

jokes.text: Rosie: 'Don't give him any water. He does this annoying thing where every time he takes a drink of water he goes, "Ah..."' / Doug: 'She does this annoying thing where every time she takes a drink of water she is an old nag.' / Leslie: 'Ah, the playful banter of a couple on the same team. That's what this is, right?'
jokes.setup: Doug asks for water before going on TV. Leslie is trying to frame the DeMarcos as a loving couple.
jokes.punchline: Rosie's complaint is petty but specific; Doug's counter-insult completely abandons specificity and just calls her an 'old nag.' Leslie's desperate reframing — 'playful banter of a couple on the same team' — is undermined by her own visible uncertainty ('That's what this is, right?').
jokes.explanation: A three-way joke where each layer adds to the comedy: Rosie's specific grievance, Doug's generalized insult, and Leslie's wishful spin. The cringe element comes from watching Leslie's dream of a harmonious merger symbol crumble in real time.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Old people are like flip phones. They're outdated, nobody uses them anymore, and they're just taking up space in the drawer.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, wait... flip phones eventually just die and nobody mourns them.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh God, I'm gonna die alone.

jokes.text: The paella cooking lesson happening in the background of the DeMarco scene — 'now you see, the trick with paella is to use just enough saffron to complement the shellfish' — while an elderly couple is fighting.
jokes.setup: The team is trying to get the DeMarcos ready for their TV interview.
jokes.punchline: A completely incongruous cooking lesson is happening simultaneously, creating a surreal juxtaposition between the earnest paella instruction and the marital discord.
jokes.explanation: A background absurdist detail that doesn't fully land on the page. The paella lesson appears to be set dressing for another segment (possibly a cooking show being taped), and the juxtaposition is mildly surreal but underdeveloped. The payoff comes later with dinner, but as a standalone moment it's weak.

dialogue.speaker: Elderly Woman
dialogue.line: I'm not touching him unless he's been drinking.

jokes.text: Leslie's desperate positive reframe: 'Ah, the playful banter of a couple on the same team. That's what this is, right?'
jokes.setup: The DeMarcos are actively hostile to each other in front of the TV crew.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's optimistic spin — calling bitter insults 'playful banter' — and her uncertain 'That's what this is, right?' reveals her plan is visibly collapsing while she tries to hold it together.
jokes.explanation: A good Leslie cringe-comedy beat. Her desperate reframing of obvious marital contempt as 'playful banter' and the uncertain tag question 'right?' are very character-true. Solid but familiar Leslie territory.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Can I get some water before we go on?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? No. Because every time you drink water, you make that sound. That gulping sound. It's so loud and annoying.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's just how people drink water.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, it's distracting. And we're about to go live on television, so maybe just... don't.

jokes.text: Rosie: 'Yeah, the uppers are kicking in. Just took some ludes to kind of smooth it out, so I'm right in that sweet spot. Got about 20 minutes before I either get really tired or really horny, so let's roll.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to get the DeMarcos ready to go on TV to represent marital bliss and Pawnee-Eagleton unity.
jokes.punchline: Rosie casually reveals a sophisticated drug cocktail and provides a clinical assessment of her pharmacological window — complete with 'really tired or really horny' as the two endpoints.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top-tier jokes. The clinical specificity of 'the uppers are kicking in, took some ludes to smooth it out' is perfectly calibrated — Rosie sounds like a pharmacist managing a portfolio. The 20-minute window with its two possible outcomes ('really tired or really horny') is both shocking and logically constructed. The juxtaposition against Leslie's desperate PR mission amplifies the comedy. The economy is excellent — no wasted words. Earns 8+ for originality (the elderly drug cocktail as pragmatic performance preparation), structure, and sheer impact.

dialogue.speaker: Wife
dialogue.line: Do you have to make that slurping sound every time you drink water?

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: Well, do you have to chew so loud? And why do you always hum while you're cooking? And could you please stop sighing every time I enter a room?

jokes.text: Doug to Rosie: 'You look like a leather glove got caught in a lawnmower.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Doug if he's sure he wants to go on TV.
jokes.punchline: Doug turns it around as an insult at Rosie — comparing her appearance to 'a leather glove caught in a lawnmower.'
jokes.explanation: A strong insult joke elevated by its specificity. 'A leather glove caught in a lawnmower' is a genuinely original image — it captures extreme weathering and damage with a specific visual that's both grotesque and funny. The misdirection of who the insult is aimed at (Leslie asked about Doug, Doug attacks Rosie) adds an extra layer.

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: Yeah, I took some uppers before we came on TV. I wanted to be sharp, you know? Really energetic.

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: But then I remembered back in '87, I took some Quaaludes with this girl named Sheila. That was a Wednesday. By Friday, I couldn't remember my own name. By Sunday, I was in a ditch outside of Reno.

jokes.text: Tom: 'How much postage does it take to send a letter to Canada?' / Ron: 'Who's it going to?' / Tom: 'Canada.' / Ron reads it: 'It says, "Dear Canada, you."'
jokes.setup: Ron has been writing strongly-worded letters. Tom asks about postage for a Canadian letter.
jokes.punchline: The letter's contents are revealed: 'Dear Canada, you.' — an incomplete sentence as a complete expression of contempt. Ron's deadpan reading of it makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: An absolutely brilliant joke in the running gag about Ron's letters. 'Dear Canada, you.' is the perfect escalation — it starts as a formal letter but the contents are an unfinished accusation that implies everything while saying nothing. The incomplete sentence IS the contempt. It suggests the writer couldn't even be bothered to articulate the complaint, or that 'you' says it all. The economy is near-perfect — two words as a letter to an entire country. The callback structure rewards attentive viewers. This is in the episode's top tier and justifies 8+ for originality, economy, and the audacity of the premise.

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: Do I look okay for TV?

dialogue.speaker: Doug's Wife
dialogue.line: You look like a thumb that gained sentience and decided to become a news anchor.

jokes.text: Doug's account of how they met: 'Well, it was 1963, and we met, and it was great.'
jokes.setup: Joan Callamezzo asks the DeMarcos to tell the romantic story of how they met — framing it as a touching moment.
jokes.punchline: Doug's summary of their origin story is the most reductive possible: they met, and it was great. 50 years compressed into one clause.
jokes.explanation: A well-timed deadpan understatement. The complete absence of romantic detail for what's supposed to be a heartwarming TV segment is the joke. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Kyle, I rejected your cat adoption application.

dialogue.speaker: Kyle
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Because you're not responsible enough. You can't even keep a plant alive.

dialogue.speaker: Kyle
dialogue.line: That's not fair!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I did it for your own good. You should be thanking me. But you're not going to, because you're fired.

jokes.text: Joan: 'What is the secret sauce that we should all be putting on our marriage burgers?' / Rosie: 'Well, we never go to bed angry.' / Joan: 'Never, ever would have thought of that.'
jokes.setup: Joan asks for the secret to a long marriage in an absurdly food-metaphorical way.
jokes.punchline: Rosie gives the most clichéd possible answer. Joan's response — 'Never, ever would have thought of that' — is a perfectly dry, devastating dismissal.
jokes.explanation: Joan's 'secret sauce on our marriage burgers' is a funny in-character question — Joan always leans into overwrought metaphor. Rosie's cliché answer sets up Joan's withering deadpan perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Kyle
dialogue.line: You can't fire me.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: You're fired.

jokes.text: Rosie's reveal of why they got married: 'I had no prospects, and Dougie here had an alcohol problem. Plus the Cold War was happening, and frankly, we all thought we were gonna die.'
jokes.setup: The TV segment is supposed to present the DeMarcos as a romantic symbol of cross-town unity.
jokes.punchline: Rosie's completely honest account of their marriage's origins: no prospects + alcoholism + Cold War fatalism = marriage. The casualness of 'frankly, we all thought we were gonna die' as a romantic context is the key laugh.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect comedy of demolition. The DeMarcos' marriage story is being set up as a romantic symbol; Rosie dismantles it in three sentences. Each element of her explanation is worse than the last — no prospects, alcoholism, nuclear anxiety — and 'frankly, we all thought we were gonna die' as a marriage motivator is bleak, honest, and perfectly delivered. The structure of escalating bad reasons works beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ron, you can't just write 'Dear America' on a letter and not put a stamp on it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why not? I'm addressing the entire country.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not how the postal system works.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Well, it should be. I have some very important things to say to these people, and most of them are about how lazy they are.

jokes.text: Doug: 'Well, I figured I could really tick off my parents by shacking up with some Pawnee trash.'
jokes.setup: Following Rosie's dispiriting account, Doug offers his own reason for marrying her.
jokes.punchline: His motivation was pure parental provocation — calling Rosie 'some Pawnee trash' as a loving/insulting characterization of his rebellious choice.
jokes.explanation: A good companion to Rosie's revelation — each spouse's account makes the marriage sound worse and more accidental. 'Some Pawnee trash' is a nice callback to the episode's merger theme while also being a comically blunt character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I don't believe in marriage. It's an antiquated concept designed by the government to control our lives.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: But if I were to get married, it would be for practical reasons only: tax benefits, someone to manage my woodworking inventory, and a legal witness to my will.

jokes.text: Leslie trying to redirect: 'We all agree that marriages have their ups and downs, but at the end of the day, they're worth it because...' / Doug: 'Who likes tap dancing?'
jokes.setup: Leslie desperately tries to salvage the TV segment with a leading question about marriage's worth.
jokes.punchline: Doug's response to what should be an earnest marriage reflection is... a question about tap dancing. A complete non-sequitur that suggests he's either not listening or chemically somewhere else.
jokes.explanation: The perfect non-sequitur response to Leslie's desperate pivot. 'Who likes tap dancing?' as an answer to a question about the value of marriage has the rhythm and surprise of a great punchline. Given the earlier ludes revelation, it also implies drug-induced tangent — adding a layer.

dialogue.speaker: Doug
dialogue.line: I married my wife purely to spite my parents and insult her town.

jokes.text: Rosie: 'I slept with Sharon in 1979.' / Doug: 'I used to get out of the shower in front of your brother on purpose.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has tried to redirect the interview to the positives. The DeMarcos are on a roll with honesty.
jokes.punchline: Two simultaneous confessions of infidelity/inappropriate behavior, delivered casually on live TV, escalating the interview disaster.
jokes.explanation: The confessional escalation works because the two reveals happen rapidly and simultaneously — Rosie's infidelity is topped by Doug's exhibitionism for her brother. The structure mirrors the form of mutual destruction. Good cringe-comedy escalation.

dialogue.line: Casual confession of decades-old adultery on live radio

jokes.text: Tom to Leslie: 'Hey, Leslie, who cares? They're old people. They eat, they sleep, they complain, and they watch Family Feud.' Leslie: 'Oh, my God, I wanna be an old person.'
jokes.setup: Tom dismisses the DeMarco disaster with a reductive description of old age.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response — rather than disagreeing — is to find the lifestyle Tom described genuinely appealing. 'Oh, my God, I wanna be an old person' reframes Tom's dismissal as an advertisement.
jokes.explanation: An unexpected pivot. Tom's description of old age is meant to be dismissive, but Leslie's exhausted sincerity — 'Oh, my God, I wanna be an old person' — is a perfect character reaction. It recontextualizes Tom's jab as an aspirational lifestyle and says a lot about how stressed Leslie is.

dialogue.speaker: Rosie
dialogue.line: Well, since we're being honest, I've been having an affair with your brother for three years.

jokes.text: A vegan restaurant owner arrives at Ron's office: he nailed the letter to the restaurant door and signed his real name and address.
jokes.setup: Ron has been writing strongly-worded letters. He signed his name and address.
jokes.punchline: The letter was physically nailed to the door (not mailed), and the owner easily found Ron because he provided his contact information at the bottom.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the letter-writing gag. 'Nailing' a letter to a door is a wonderfully Ron Swanson detail — medieval, decisive, and theatrical. His unabashed ownership of the action ('Because I believe it. Good day.') and complete indifference to consequences is perfect character work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know, playing shuffleboard, early bird specials, napping at 3 PM... Wait. Why does that sound amazing?

jokes.text: Ron: 'A vegan is gonna physically attack me? They're basically made of glass. But more importantly, if you believe in something, you sign your name to it.'
jokes.setup: April asks how the vegan restaurant owner found him.
jokes.punchline: Ron dismisses the physical threat from vegans ('basically made of glass') and then pivots to a principled defense of signing your name — the contrast between contemptuous dismissal and genuine moral conviction is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'They're basically made of glass' is a perfectly absurd dismissal of vegans' physical threat level, calibrated to Ron's meat-centric worldview. The pivot to genuine moral principle ('if you believe in something, you sign your name to it') is what makes this exceptional — Ron seamlessly goes from contemptuous insult to noble declaration. It's funny AND it's sincere Ron Swanson philosophy. The contrast between the two clauses is the key. Earns 8+ for character integration and the sophistication of the two-clause structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Dear Vegetable Garden Restaurant, I have nothing but contempt for your philosophy. Eating a meal without meat is like watching television without sound. It's pointless and makes me angry. However, I will be dining at your establishment this Friday evening. My son is graduating, and his mother insists we celebrate at your restaurant. I have only one request: prepare the largest steak you have. If you do not have steak, prepare the largest block of cheese you have. I will eat nothing else. Sincerely, Ron Swanson.

jokes.text: Ron: 'But more importantly, if you believe in something, you sign your name to it. Which is why the makers of carbonated water will soon know exactly where to find me.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just explained why he signed his real name to his letters.
jokes.punchline: Ron frames his courageous transparency as a principled stance — then reveals the next target is carbonated water manufacturers. The escalating letter campaign continues.
jokes.explanation: A good running gag payoff. The juxtaposition of Ron's principled stance on personal accountability with his enemies list (which apparently includes carbonated water) is the joke. His righteous certainty about such trivial grievances is consistently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What are you afraid of? That they'll come after you? Have you seen a vegan? They're all like 110 pounds and very pale. I could take on six vegans with my bare hands tied behind my back. Actually, I could take on six vegans with my bare hands tied in front of my back.

jokes.text: Donna reveals she knew it was Tom who wrote the review — because another review from the same account said 'Great first date spot' about a funeral home.
jokes.setup: Tom confesses he wrote the Yelp review. Donna says she already knew.
jokes.punchline: The tell was a funeral home review calling it a 'great first date spot' — which is such a Tom Haverford move that it immediately identified the account.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly constructed callback and reveal. The 'great first date spot' for a funeral home is funny as a standalone Tom concept — morbid, unconventional, weirdly confident — but it working as a fingerprint that blows his anonymous cover makes it structurally elegant. High character integration: only Tom Haverford would review a funeral home as a date venue AND be undone by that review.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I knew it was April because only April would write a fake review saying 'This funeral home gave me chills... and not in a good way.'

jokes.text: Tom: 'Well, you overestimated how much I care what happens to Kyle. Or anyone, really.'
jokes.setup: Donna dragged in Kyle expecting Tom to feel guilty when she threatened to fire him.
jokes.punchline: Tom admits he felt nothing about Kyle's predicament — and extends this to 'anyone, really' with complete calm.
jokes.explanation: Tom's casual sociopathy toward Kyle (and everyone) is a reliable character beat, but the 'or anyone, really' extension makes it funnier than standard Tom selfishness.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Your outfit today is really not working for you.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Okay, we're done being direct.

jokes.text: Donna and Tom reconcile: 'From now on, we say what we feel. Cool?' / 'Cool.' / 'Your lipstick looks weird.' / 'You're gonna want to shut your mouth right now.'
jokes.setup: Donna and Tom agree to be direct with each other going forward.
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately exercises their new policy by pointing out Donna's lipstick — and Donna immediately threatens him for it. Their 'directness' pact collapses within seconds.
jokes.explanation: A tight three-exchange joke. The comedic premise (their agreement to be direct is immediately tested and immediately fails) is well-structured, and both characters behave exactly as you'd expect. The speed of the collapse — one sentence into the new arrangement — is the key to its effectiveness. 'Good talk.' as a button is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I have a split personality. There's Craig, who's a gentle soul who loves Sex and the City, and then there's the other Craig, who will cut you.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Maybe Pawneeans and Eagletonians aren't meant to coexist.' / Ben and Larry clink glasses: 'At least our merger is going well.' / 'Cheers.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is demoralized about the merger after the DeMarco disaster.
jokes.punchline: Ben and Larry, who have spent the episode on a ridiculous day together, comment on their unexpected 'merger.' The joke is that their forced pairing worked out better than the actual civic merger.
jokes.explanation: A nice thematic button that also works as a warm Ben/Larry character moment. The merger language doubles effectively, though it's more of a pleasant moment than a big laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: We're trying to book an R&B singer for the Unity Concert. If we can actually get someone big, it could be life-changing for this whole department.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I'm talking about the kind of impact that makes people remember where they were when they heard the announcement.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'The children are our future. Whitney Houston knew it, and so do you, and so do I.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has realized the solution to the merger problem is the youth.
jokes.punchline: Leslie attributes this insight to Whitney Houston (via the song 'Greatest Love of All') as though it's a serious policy citation, combining her earnestness with her pop culture reverence.
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie: earnest, policy-minded statement delivered through the lens of a pop song with complete sincerity. Works as character comedy though not particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A Unity Concert? That's... I... we could... the whole town... everyone together... music and... oh my god, oh my god, oh my god!

jokes.text: Craig's introduction: 'Craig Middlebrooks. Samantha in the boardroom, Miranda in the bedroom. I know it's not ideal, but it's who I am.'
jokes.setup: New committee members introduce themselves.
jokes.punchline: Craig's self-description as 'Samantha in the boardroom, Miranda in the bedroom' (Sex and the City character types) is an outrageously specific overshare for a professional introduction. 'I know it's not ideal, but it's who I am' sells it with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: A stellar character introduction. The Sex and the City SATC framing is specific enough to reward those who know it while the joke still lands as pure oversharing absurdity for those who don't. 'I know it's not ideal, but it's who I am' is both funny (treating this as a character flaw he's learned to accept) and perfectly delivered as sincere self-acceptance. A great first impression for a recurring character. Earns 8+ for originality and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Woop woop woop! Oh my God, yes! Mmmmph! Whee!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: She's excited about something.

jokes.text: Madison's introduction: 'This is my friend Madison. She's amazing. And she drove me here!'
jokes.setup: Introductions continue. Andy introduces his friend.
jokes.punchline: The climactic credential Andy offers for Madison is that she drove him — not any skill, expertise, or relevant qualification. The exclamation point suggests he finds this genuinely impressive.
jokes.explanation: Andy's standard of excellence ('she drove me here!') is perfectly calibrated to his character. The exclamation implies genuine admiration for the most basic act of transportation. Quick, economical, character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God. Oh my—Ben, this is... I can't even... This is the most beautiful thing I've ever seen and I'm going to cry and also I might throw up, but like, in a good way.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You son of a—gun. You beautiful son of a gun.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'You get to B.S.-ing, brainstorming. Just chill. Peace out.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to speak to young people in their language.
jokes.punchline: Her youth-adjacent language ('just chill, peace out') is delivered with the energy and cadence of a government official, making it both dorky and endearing. 'B.S.-ing, brainstorming' is the comedic peak.
jokes.explanation: A reliable Leslie-trying-to-be-cool joke. 'B.S.-ing, brainstorming' is the best part — she can't quite commit to the profanity even in slang form. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I got you something. It's the Iron Throne from Game of Thrones, but it's a replica made by this artisan who's been a fan since before the books were even published.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, this is incredible. How did you even find someone who could make this?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I may have spent the last three months tracking down the most dedicated Game of Thrones fan in the tri-state area. And when I say dedicated, I mean this person has read all the books multiple times, watches the show, has attended every Comic-Con since 2011, and once drove seventeen hours just to visit the filming locations in Croatia.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... that's a lot of dedication.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah. Oh, and they're also my mom.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'You need to figure out how to hold this town together. You are going to meet twice a week and you're here because of your energy, and your youth, and for some of you, your mental age.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is laying out the committee's mandate.
jokes.punchline: 'For some of you, your mental age' — an aside acknowledging that at least one committee member (probably Craig) is not actually young, but has been included on the basis of emotional/mental youth.
jokes.explanation: A good aside. 'For some of you, your mental age' is a well-placed callback to Craig being an adult in a youth meeting. The parenthetical structure is efficient and the implication is clear without being belabored.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Winter is coming.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Actually, the line is 'The winters are coming.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, it's definitely 'Winter is coming.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm pretty sure there's an article. 'The winters are coming.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, I'm sitting on the Iron Throne. I think I know what I'm talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, please, you're quoting it wrong! It's 'The winters are coming!' THE WINTERS! It's a metaphor for multiple hardships!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Winter. Singular. Is. Coming.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: NO! NO NO NO! You're ruining Game of Thrones! You're ruining television! You're ruining WINTER!

jokes.text: Leslie's second attempt to read the room: "So it's been an hour... it looks like you guys were having some fun... so why don't we call this first meeting a success and then we'll get together later in the week." / "Hold up, sweet pea. We have an idea."
jokes.setup: Leslie has given the youth committee an hour and is ready to call it a win.
jokes.punchline: She massively underestimated them — they produced a massive, fully-formed Unity Concert concept in one hour.
jokes.explanation: A decent reversal — Leslie's low expectations are demolished. 'Hold up, sweet pea' from Craig is very him. The joke functions as a plot beat as much as a comedic one.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And that's why we should adopt the Stark family motto for our department: 'Winter is Coming.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's Game of Thrones.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Right, the one with all the dragons and the throne made of swords. Very inspiring for government work.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Please stop talking about franchises you haven't watched.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? I watched it. I watched at least twenty minutes of it on an airplane once.

jokes.text: 'It's gonna be like a giant Woodstock, except for instead of everybody rolling around in mud, they'll be rolling around in happiness. Or maybe mud. I don't know. I can't control the weather.'
jokes.setup: Craig is pitching the Unity Concert concept to Leslie.
jokes.punchline: The Woodstock comparison is immediately complicated by his acknowledgment that he cannot control weather — the earnest disclaimer 'I can't control the weather' undercuts the grand vision with pragmatic uncertainty.
jokes.explanation: Craig's earnest pivot from inspirational metaphor to meteorological disclaimer is a good character joke. The logic of 'maybe mud, I don't know, I can't control the weather' is disarmingly honest and funny.

jokes.text: 'Donna said she might be able to get Ginuwine. That's given me a reason to live.'
jokes.setup: The committee is listing attractions for the festival.
jokes.punchline: Craig's enthusiasm for Ginuwine as a performer escalates to existential — 'that's given me a reason to live' implies his previous state was one of profound meaninglessness.
jokes.explanation: Craig's outsized emotional response to Ginuwine's potential availability is a great character moment — his intensity is both funny and oddly moving. The jump from 'might get Ginuwine' to 'reason to live' is a perfect escalation in minimal words.

jokes.text: Leslie responds to the Unity Concert pitch by making inarticulate noises ('I don't... I don't... I don't even... You know what I mean?') — bystanders ask 'What's wrong with her? Why is she making those noises?' / Response: 'That means she loves it so much she can't speak.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just heard a perfect pitch that solves all her problems.
jokes.punchline: Her response is pure emotional overflow — inarticulate sounds — which to an outsider looks alarming but to those who know Leslie is the highest form of praise.
jokes.explanation: A strong character moment: Leslie's enthusiasm overloading her verbal capacity is perfect, and the outside observer's alarm vs. Andy's knowing explanation creates a warm double-perspective joke. High character integration.

jokes.text: Ben's elaborate anniversary reveal: enchanted carriage, scrapbook, multiple gifts — and Leslie's comment: 'Oh, and your scrapbook instincts are really good. I mean, this is a little rough, but you have a lot of talent here.'
jokes.setup: Ben has pulled off an elaborate surprise. Leslie is overwhelmed and touched.
jokes.punchline: In the midst of her emotional response, Leslie can't help but critique his scrapbooking — praising his instincts while also calling it 'a little rough.' She can't turn off the expert even when genuinely moved.
jokes.explanation: Leslie critiquing Ben's scrapbooking in the middle of a romantic moment is a perfect character beat — she's moved, but she's also a scrapbooking professional and cannot withhold professional assessment. 'A lot of talent here' as encouraging note is both funny and warm.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Oh, I can't believe I actually defeated Leslie Knope at a gift exchange. Yes!'
jokes.setup: Ben thinks he's finally won the annual gift-surprise competition.
jokes.punchline: His framing of this as 'defeating Leslie Knope' — as though it's a military campaign — and his fist-pump victory celebration is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A good callback payoff to the episode's opening gift-battle setup. Ben's premature victory celebration is perfectly timed for the incoming reversal.

jokes.text: Leslie reveals the Iron Throne replica. Ben's reaction: 'Ohh! It's the Iron Throne.'
jokes.setup: Ben thought he won the gift exchange. Leslie has one more gift.
jokes.punchline: The Iron Throne — a handmade replica of the Game of Thrones seat of power — is the ultimate Ben Wyatt gift, completely unexpected and perfectly calibrated to his nerd sensibilities. His ecstatic repetition is the reaction.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the episode's central comedic throughline. The structure is beautifully earned: we've spent 20 minutes waiting to see who makes 'the face' and who wins the gift battle. The Iron Throne is the perfect final revelation — it's so specifically Ben that the audience feels the same delight he does. The callback to the episode's framing completes with a satisfying click. High marks for structure and character integration. The scene where Ben sits on it and tries to do Game of Thrones dialogue pushes this even further.

jokes.text: The Iron Throne reveal — Leslie has had a model replica of the Game of Thrones Iron Throne made for Ben. His face drops into the 'stupid face.'
jokes.setup: Ben has just gloated about defeating Leslie. She reveals her gift.
jokes.punchline: The Iron Throne is the perfect gift for Ben — and Ben immediately makes 'that stupid face,' completing the episode's central callback.
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the episode's main comedic through-line. The Iron Throne is perfectly calibrated to Ben's character (Game of Thrones superfan), and its arrival — after Ben has just claimed victory — delivers the 'stupid face' the episode has been building to. Ben's 'Okay, I know I'm making that dumb surprise face, but I can't help it' acknowledging the callback explicitly is a nice touch. The structure is very clean: the episode earns this moment.

jokes.text: Ben sits on the Iron Throne: 'When you play the game of thrones, you win or you die.' / Leslie: 'Yes.' / Ben: 'No.' / Leslie: 'Yes.' / Ben: 'No!' / 'Come here. Come hither, peasant. Come here. Who are you?' / Leslie: 'Our starship is in trouble.' / Ben: 'Okay, Leslie, listen. If you're not... if you don't know what you're talking about...'
jokes.setup: Ben is ecstatic about the Iron Throne. He starts roleplaying Game of Thrones while Leslie tries to join in.
jokes.punchline: Leslie mixes up her sci-fi franchises ('our starship is in trouble' is Star Trek/Wars, not GoT), and Ben — despite the romantic moment — cannot let the franchise confusion stand.
jokes.explanation: The closing joke of the episode is a perfect character button. Ben's Game of Thrones enthusiasm runs into Leslie's genre confusion — she conflates space opera with fantasy — and Ben's correction instinct overrides his romantic moment. 'Okay, Leslie, listen...' is the perfect ending line: Ben's pedantry winning over his feelings. Both characters behave exactly as they should. 'Come hither, peasant' is also quotable. High character integration for both.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Come here. Come hither, peasant. Come here. Who are you?' Leslie: 'Our starship is in trouble.'
jokes.setup: Ben is fully in Game of Thrones mode, beckoning Leslie with medieval language.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response — 'Our starship is in trouble' — is from a completely different sci-fi franchise (Star Trek), revealing that she's been trying to improvise genre fiction and mixed up her fantasy universes.
jokes.explanation: A lovely closing joke. Leslie has tried to participate in Ben's Game of Thrones moment and defaulted to Star Trek — revealing she's operating from a general 'sci-fi stuff' bucket with no specificity. Ben's exasperated 'Okay, Leslie, listen. If you're not... if you don't know what you're talking about...' as the episode's final line is a perfect button.

tmdb_overview: Leslie's efforts to take down the wall separating Eagleton and Pawnee yield unexpected results; Ben and Tom meet with possible sponsors for the concert; Ron finds a new hobby.
insight: Solid character work carries 66 jokes through three parallel anniversary threads without standout peaks.
